case_study_insert.main_stem: Calderline Freight (CLF) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by Derek Calder, the business operates regional haulage routes between distribution warehouses and supermarkets, using a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CLF plans to invest $640,000 in 14 electric trucks and a charging depot, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $209,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.70, and produces 65,000 units a year (each unit being one completed delivery contract). CLF faces a shortage of licensed heavy truck drivers, with overtime now running at 14% of wage costs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — October 2026: The fleet completed 5,400 delivery contracts last month with 96.2% on-time performance, down from 98.1% in April. Average diesel cost was $0.92 per mile. Two truck breakdowns caused 37 late deliveries. A customer survey of 340 contracted shippers found that 71% would pay a 4% surcharge for guaranteed carbon-neutral deliveries, and 58% said live tracking transparency influences contract renewal. Driver overtime averaged 14% of wage costs. Off-the-job eco-driving certification courses cost $450 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Calderline Freight for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, the third rise this year, increasing repayments on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.80 to $12.50 per hour from April 2027, lifting fleet wage bills. (3) Diesel and AdBlue input costs have risen 15.2% year-on-year, while retail diesel prices pushed operating budgets up 9.6%, even as road freight demand grew 2.8% across the region.

questions.question_text: CLF plans to finance its $640,000 electric truck expansion partly with $240,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for CLF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the $400,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs CLF nothing in interest or repayments, which is vital while it already services fixed costs of $209,000 a year and faces a 15.2% rise in diesel input costs. Keeping the $240,000 free of repayment pressure protects the company's cash flow and operating profit margin, so the carbon-neutral electric trucks can bed in without the strain of servicing extra debt on top of the $400,000 seven-year loan. Every dollar retained rather than paid as loan interest can absorb fuel volatility or help underwrite the 4% surcharge that 71% of surveyed shippers say they will accept.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids additional collateral and the risk of the bank imposing covenants or repossessing the new charging depot and trucks if demand disappoints. Because the trucks are central to CLF's plan to win guaranteed carbon-neutral supermarket contracts, protecting title to them safeguards future revenue and Derek Calder's autocratic control over how the $640,000 is deployed. Retained profit also needs no credit approval, so CLF can order the 14 electric trucks quickly and move ahead of rivals before the 5.75% interest rate makes external borrowing more expensive.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CLF's expansion, costs and rising input prices.

questions.question_text: CLF is launching its guaranteed carbon-neutral delivery service for supermarket and warehouse contracts. Consider a national television campaign, full-page adverts in a regional newspaper, or targeted business-to-business marketing on LinkedIn to logistics managers. Which should CLF choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A national TV campaign would make CLF instantly visible across the region and would help build general awareness of carbon-neutral haulage. However, production and airtime costs are extremely high, a large share of the audience would never buy contracted freight, and the message cannot easily be tailored to the 340 shippers in its survey. For a 52-employee business that has just committed $640,000 to electric trucks and carries $209,000 of fixed costs, this would be an unaffordable and untargeted gamble.

Regional newspaper advertising: Full-page adverts in the regional newspaper are far cheaper than television, reach a local audience, and suit a message about cleaner regional routes. The limitation is that shippers and logistics managers — the decision-makers behind CLF's contracted routes — are a tiny fraction of the readership, so most spend would be wasted on consumers, and response would be hard to track against the 96.2% on-time-performance story CLF most wants to tell.

LinkedIn business-to-business marketing: Targeted campaigns can reach supermarket procurement and warehouse logistics managers directly, share the 71% surcharge finding and 58% tracking-transparency research, attach route maps and case studies, and measure click-throughs cost-effectively. Reach is smaller than TV but precisely on-target, and costs are modest relative to $640,000 of committed capital.

Recommendation: CLF should choose targeted business-to-business marketing on LinkedIn. It reaches exactly the decision-makers who renew supermarket and distribution contracts, communicates the carbon-neutral and tracking benefits with proof, and costs a fraction of television. Television is rejected as too broad and too expensive for a 52-employee hauler; regional newspaper advertising is rejected as poorly targeted at freight buyers and hard to measure, though CLF could add a small local print presence as support once contract wins justify it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to CLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of CLF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CLF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspaper advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: CLF's driver shortage has pushed overtime to 14% of wage costs and 37 late deliveries followed two breakdowns. Explain two benefits for CLF of introducing a retention bonus scheme for its heavy truck drivers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A retention bonus gives drivers a tangible financial reason to stay with CLF rather than move to rival hauliers during the national driver shortage, reducing labour turnover and the cost of recruiting and inducting replacement drivers. Stable staffing protects the 96.2% on-time performance that shippers expect, and fewer late deliveries means fewer penalty clauses on supermarket contracts and less pressure on the 14% overtime bill that is eroding route margins.

Point 2: Knowing their pay is linked to staying also encourages drivers to look after the new electric trucks and follow eco-driving standards, helping the 4% surcharge-backed carbon-neutral promise hold up and reducing breakdown-related disruption like the two failures that caused 37 late deliveries. Lower turnover also preserves CLF's experience base, so routes are run efficiently even while the charging depot is being commissioned, supporting the hierarchical operation Derek Calder wants under autocratic control and keeping total output on course for 65,000 completed contracts a year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CLF's driver shortage, overtime and service reliability.

questions.question_text: CLF must close its licensed heavy truck driver shortage and cut the 14% overtime bill. Consider recruiting experienced drivers externally through a specialist agency, or retraining reliable warehouse staff into driving roles through off-the-job certification at $450 per driver. Which should CLF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External agency recruitment: Using a licensed driver agency fills vacancies fast, which CLF needs while overtime runs at 14% of wage costs and on-time performance has slipped to 96.2%. Agency drivers arrive qualified and insured, so compliance is immediate. However, agency fees are high, temp drivers lack loyalty to CLF's culture and its 14 new electric trucks, and they leave as soon as permanent roles open elsewhere, so continuity, safe eco-driving habits and the carbon-neutral surcharge promise are all put at risk.

Off-the-job certification of warehouse staff: Training internal staff at $450 per driver turns known, trusted employees into qualified drivers, builds loyalty consistent with autocratic but stable management, and is far cheaper than perpetual agency fees. Drawbacks are time — warehouse staff still need the hours and licensing checks before they can drive heavy trucks — and a temporary gap in the depot while they train, which could worsen the 37 late deliveries problem in the short term.

Decision: CLF should choose off-the-job certification of warehouse staff, while keeping a small number of agency drivers only as a temporary bridge. The $450 per head cost is minimal against the $640,000 expansion, it converts existing reliable staff into long-term assets, and it attacks the root cause of the shortage rather than renting it. Pure agency recruitment is rejected as a permanent solution because fees would deepen the overtime-and-cost crisis and do nothing for retention, safety culture or the carbon-neutral service; a hybrid short-term agency cover remains acceptable until the first certified cohort qualifies.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to CLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of CLF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of CLF with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, safety culture and retention.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CLF's management can use its cost, break-even and delivery data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $209,000 ÷ ($12.70 − $7.20) = $209,000 ÷ $5.50 = 38,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 38,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.70 − $7.20 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CLF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CLF can compare the 38,000-unit break-even output with its 65,000 completed contracts to confirm a margin of safety of 27,000 units, showing the $640,000 expansion is comfortably covered and helping set route-growth targets before committing to more vehicles.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.50 lets managers model supermarket tariff negotiations, for example whether accepting a 4% surcharge on a lower base price still covers the $209,000 fixed costs and $400,000 bank loan repayments.
3. Knowing contribution and fixed costs helps CLF stress-test the effect of the 15.2% diesel cost rise, since a higher $7.20 variable cost shrinks $5.50 contribution directly, warning managers early to renegotiate rates or accelerate the electric fleet rollout.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost — fixed cost per unit of $209,000 ÷ 65,000 = $3.22 plus variable cost, giving $10.42 a unit — to spot depot waste, push delivery contracts toward $12.70, and identify which of the 5,400 monthly contracts are actually profitable.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 38,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 27,000 units vs 65,000 contracts; tariff and surcharge modelling to protect $5.50 contribution; stress-testing loan feasibility against the 15.2% diesel rise; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.42 to cut waste and protect contract pricing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CLF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CLF's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 42.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 46.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $2,400,000 revenue − $1,392,000 cost of sales = $1,008,000, giving $1,008,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 42.0%; 2025 = ($2,750,000 − $1,485,000) = $1,265,000 ÷ $2,750,000 = 46.0%. Profitability after operating expenses: 2024 $288,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 12.0%; 2025 $385,000 ÷ $2,750,000 = 14.0%. Efficiency of capital use: 2024 $288,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 16.0%; 2025 $385,000 ÷ $2,200,000 = 17.5%.

Evaluation: Performance has clearly strengthened. The trading margin widened from 42.0% to 46.0%, helped by better route density and the carbon-neutral surcharge, and operating performance improved from 12.0% to 14.0% despite interest payable rising from $54,000 to $66,000 as the $400,000 bank loan was drawn. Capital efficiency also improved from 16.0% to 17.5% even though capital employed grew by $400,000 to $2,200,000, suggesting the 14 electric trucks are already generating returns above their financing cost. However, cost of sales still grew from $1,392,000 to $1,485,000 alongside the 15.2% diesel rise, and the expansion has raised fixed financing commitments; if the shipped-contract mix shifts toward lower-surcharge work, the 46.0% figure could erode quickly.

Conclusion: CLF's financial performance has improved. Trading margins rose from 42.0% to 46.0%, operating returns from 12.0% to 14.0%, and capital efficiency from 16.0% to 17.5%, all with higher revenue of $2,750,000. The improvement is genuine but not guaranteed to last, so CLF should lock in surcharge clauses, fix diesel hedging where possible, and monitor capital use before funding further fleet purchases with more debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether CLF has improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CLF of switching its regional fleet to electric trucks powered by renewable electricity.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Electric trucks directly enable CLF's guaranteed carbon-neutral delivery promise, the very service its survey shows 71% of shippers would pay a 4% surcharge for, so CLF can charge premium rates that protect the $5.50 contribution per completed contract even as diesel costs rise 15.2%. Renewable-powered vehicles also cut exposure to diesel price volatility, deal with the 9.6% rise in retail diesel budgets, and strengthen CLF's image when bidding for supermarket fleets that rank sustainability highly, supporting the $640,000 business case.

Disadvantage: The upfront cost of $640,000 for 14 trucks and a charging depot is heavy for a 52-employee business already carrying a $400,000 seven-year bank loan, and charging infrastructure still needs commissioning, which could disrupt route reliability while on-time performance has already slipped to 96.2%. Electric trucks also range-limit long hauls and depend on charging-depot uptime, so any outage could multiply late deliveries beyond the 37 already recorded, and resale values remain uncertain if battery technology moves quickly.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CLF's expansion, contracts and fuel exposure.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.75%, the 5.9% increase in the minimum wage to $12.50 and the 15.2% rise in diesel and AdBlue input costs will affect CLF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If CLF's $400,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% increase adds roughly $3,000 a year to financing costs, slightly deepening the rise in interest payable from $54,000 to $66,000 seen in 2025. Higher rates also raise the hurdle for any future fleet borrowing and may make some shippers more cautious about committing to long contracts. The direct cash impact is real but modest, and CLF can mitigate it by fixing the loan rate or renegotiating terms.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.50 per hour from April 2027): CLF's 52-strong workforce is concentrated in driving and depot work. The insert gives the new floor at $12.50 per hour, up $0.70 from $11.80, so every employee paid at the minimum gains about $0.70 an hour; on top of 14% overtime this squeezes the $5.50 contribution unless the 4% carbon-neutral surcharge and route repricing are passed through. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely — but the rise falls broadly across the workforce and will recur every year. However, CLF can offset much of it through productivity and scheduling gains as the electric depot comes on line, and it partly protects morale, aiding the retention-bonus fight against the driver shortage.

Diesel and AdBlue input cost inflation (15.2%): Fuel is embedded in the $7.20 variable cost of every one of the 65,000 contracts CLF produces. With road-freight demand still growing just 2.8% and retail diesel prices pushing operating budgets up 9.6%, a 15.2% year-on-year rise feeds straight into every contract CLF completes, directly eroding the $5.50 contribution. The insert does not decompose the variable cost, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely; for illustration only, if the fuel-linked portion were $0.50 per unit, a 15.2% rise on it would add about $0.08 per unit, and at 65,000 units that is roughly $5,000 a year — illustrative only. Even so, the rise compounds on every unit and damages the 96.2% on-time economics of every route, striking precisely the margin that justifies the $640,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 15.2% rise in diesel and AdBlue input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit CLF produces, feeds straight into the $7.20 variable cost and the $5.50 contribution, and cannot be fully recovered without risking contracts in a competitive market. The wage increase is significant but more manageable through productivity and surcharges, and the interest-rate rise is the smallest cash impact and can be fixed. CLF should prioritise fuel hedging, route repricing and accelerating the electric fleet to dilute diesel exposure.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CLF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CLF with a well-justified judgement that diesel and AdBlue inflation has the greatest impact.
